etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English vicious, from Anglo-Norman vicious, (modern French vicieux), from Latin vitiōsus, from vitium (“fault, vice”). Equivalent to vice +‎ -ous.

quote.citation: 1922, Michael Arlen, “2/9/1”, in “Piracy”: A Romantic Chronicle of These Days:
quote.text: He had always been remarkably immune from such little ailments, and had only once in his life been ill, of a vicious pneumonia long ago at school. He hadn't the faintest idea what to with a cold in the head, he just took quinine and continued to blow his nose.

definitions.definition: (archaic) Pertaining to vice; characterised by immorality or depravity.

quote.text: We may so seize on vertue, that if we embrace it with an over-greedy and violent desire, it may become vicious.

quote.citation: 1930, Ogden Nash, Lines to Be Mumbled at Ovington's:
quote.text: A murrain on you, Reverend Apse/I hope you get caught in a vicious moral lapse.
